strengths: The paper presents a unified, training-free inference-time framework (AIS + SMC) for composing heterogeneous knowledge sources — generative flow/diffusion experts, discriminative VLM rewards, and non-neural physics simulators — which is a natural and useful generalization of prior SMC-based reward steering ([46, 55]) and compositional generative modeling ([11, 41]).

The framework is instantiated across three distinct task families (graphics-engine-instructed image editing, physics-simulator-instructed video generation, regional text-to-image composition), demonstrating breadth and flexibility of the expert composition formulation, including region-level experts and a conditional sampling heuristic (Eq. 7) that improves visual harmonization in an ablation (Table 1, 'No Cond').

Implementation details, hyperparameters, and compute costs (4–30 min/sample on H200s) are disclosed, and the paper honestly discusses limitations (extra computation, compatibility assumptions, small expert sets), which aids reproducibility and transparency.

The qualitative results (Figs. 1–3, 5–7) show a genuinely useful capability — inserting physically plausible, simulator-driven objects/motions into natural images/videos — that monolithic baselines (RF-Solver, I2V/D2V/Traj2V) fail to achieve.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core sampling machinery is a fairly direct application of AIS and SMC to products of flow-model intermediate distributions; the delta over Du & Kaelbling [11], Thornton et al. [41], and Wu et al. [46] is mainly engineering of heterogeneous expert combinations and a heuristic conditional-sampling update (Eq. 7) whose justification (Appendix D.2) is informal rather than principled.

Quantitative evaluation is weak and small-scale: 30 image-editing scenes and 12 video scenes on custom, non-standard datasets, no human evaluation, and heavy reliance on proxy metrics (LPIPS against simulator renderings, background MSE, GPT-4o-as-judge) whose validity is not established. Several results understate the paper's claims: in Table 2 (object-centric), the LPIPS gains over Depth2V are within noise (0.104 vs. 0.103), and in Table 1 improvements in controllability are modest relative to the large standard deviations.

The central algorithmic contribution (SMC particle-based resampling with discriminative experts) is barely evaluated quantitatively: the main image/video experiments use L=1 (Appendix F.2/F.3), meaning the SMC resampling machinery is effectively inactive in Tables 1–2. The only multi-particle experiment (Section 4.4) is purely qualitative with no numerical comparison, leaving the key claim of 'sample-efficient' compositional sampling unsupported.

Sampler correctness is under-justified: Euler flow steps admittedly do not sample from p_t, only 1 MCMC step per annealing iteration is used, and intermediate reward weights r_t(x) ≈ r(x̂) are approximations; no analysis of bias, particle degeneracy, or annealing-schedule sensitivity is provided, so it is unclear the method actually targets the stated product distribution.

Baselines are incomplete: despite citing a rich related-work section, no comparison against strong training-free guidance methods (e.g., TFG, FreeDoM, universal guidance, FPS) or other SMC-based steering baselines, making it hard to attribute gains to the PoE framework rather than to the choice of FLUX/Wan backbones and conditioning signals.

The text-to-image composition experiment (Section 4.4) uses only cherry-picked examples without quantitative results on standard compositional benchmarks (e.g., GenAI-Bench metrics are cited but not reported), and the best-of-N compute-matched comparison is not backed by numbers.

Significant compute overhead (4–30 minutes per sample, multiple H200s) versus feedforward baselines is not quantified against the achieved quality gains, weakening the practical significance argument.

strengths: The paper presents a clean, unified probabilistic formulation (PoE with AIS/SMC) for composing heterogeneous experts—generative diffusion/flow models, discriminative VLMs, and non-neural physics simulators—which is an attractive and timely direction for inference-time controllable generation.

The framework is training-free and modular, and the applications (graphics-engine-instructed image editing, physics-simulator-instructed video generation, regional text-to-image composition) are interesting demonstrations of flexible control interfaces.
The conditional generative expert construction (Eq. 7) is a reasonable idea for reducing multi-modality, and there is a small ablation (Table 1, 'No Cond') supporting it.
The paper is generally well written, with implementation details and an autoregressive instantiation provided in the appendix, and it discusses limitations and compute costs openly.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: the core algorithm is a fairly direct application of Annealed Importance Sampling / Sequential Monte Carlo to product-of-experts sampling, and the paper itself states it 'builds on top of' existing SMC-based reward-steering formulations (Wu et al. 2023, Zhao et al. 2024) and generalizes compositional generation work (Du & Kaelbling 2024, Li et al. 2022, Thornton et al. 2025). The conceptual delta over this line of work is incremental.

The evaluation is far too small to support the claims at a top-tier venue: 30 scenes for image editing, 12 scenes for video generation, and only 2 qualitative example prompts for the text-to-image composition task (Fig. 6), which has no quantitative benchmark despite citing GenAI-Bench. No statistical significance testing is provided despite these tiny sample sizes.

Results are weak or internally inconsistent: in Table 1, the aesthetic score is lower than the RF-Solver baseline and LPIPS(fg) is identical for 'Ours' and 'No Cond'; several Table 2 metrics are within noise of baselines (e.g., LPIPS for object-centric simulation). The headline 'better controllability' claim rests on small margins and GPT-4o-as-judge scores, which are noisy and unverifiable.

Baselines are not the strongest or most appropriate: RF-Solver is an inversion-based editing method given only a coarse prompt, and the video baselines are just monolithic conditioning variants of the same backbone. The most natural competitors—training-free guidance/reward-steering methods for diffusion models (Universal Guidance, TFG, FreeDoM, loss-guided diffusion)—are discussed in related work but not compared against experimentally.

Algorithmic soundness concerns: Algorithm 1's Euler-step transition kernel is a Dirac delta that does not target the annealed distribution (acknowledged as an 'initialization'), the intermediate discriminative reward r_t(x) ≈ r(ˆx) via flow-endpoint prediction is an uncontrolled approximation, and with L=1 particles in most experiments (Appendix F) the SMC machinery effectively degenerates, undermining the claim that parallel sampling with resampling is the key ingredient.

Very high compute cost (4–30 minutes per sample on 1–2 H200 GPUs) is acknowledged but not quantitatively justified against cheaper baselines under matched compute; the compute-matched best-of-N comparison appears only qualitatively for one task.

The paper validates 'empirical results with small number of experts' and defers large-scale PoE sampling to future work, so the central claim of practical, scalable knowledge composition is only weakly supported.

strengths: The paper presents a unified, training-free framework for composing heterogeneous knowledge sources (flow/diffusion generative priors, VLM-based discriminative rewards, and classical physics simulators) in a single probabilistic Product-of-Experts formulation, which is a sensible and timely extension of compositional generative modeling.

The AIS/SMC-based sampler is well-motivated: it avoids the vanishing acceptance rates of rejection sampling, requires only black-box likelihood access to discriminative experts, and the conditional generative expert trick (Eq. 7) is a thoughtful practical contribution with an ablation supporting it.

Experiments span three distinct tasks (graphics-engine-instructed image editing, physics-simulator-instructed video generation, regional text-to-image composition), demonstrating breadth of the framework, and include reasonably chosen monolithic baselines (RF-Solver, Image2V, Depth2V, Traj2V, PhysGen3D) sharing backbones where possible.
An autoregressive instantiation (Appendix C, FramePack/HunyuanVideo) shows the framework is not tied to flow models, strengthening generality claims.
The paper is honest about limitations (compute overhead, expert compatibility assumptions, small-scale validation) and provides implementation details sufficient for reproduction in Appendix F.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the core machinery is a direct combination of well-known components (Neal's AIS, SMC resampling à la Doucet et al., twisted/SMC steering from Wu et al. [46] and Zhao et al. [55], and PoE composition from Du & Kaelbling [11] and Li et al. [28]). The contribution is largely an application-level generalization, and positioning relative to concurrent work [41] deserves deeper differentiation.

Evaluation scale is very small: 30 image scenes, 12 video scenes, and 9 PhysGen3D scenes. Reported standard deviations are large (e.g., GPT-4o scores ±0.10–0.22), and no statistical significance tests are provided, so many of the quantitative margins (e.g., MSE 1.429 vs. 1.511, LPIPS 0.104 vs. 0.103 in Table 2) are not clearly meaningful.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4o as an automatic judge on the model's own outputs raises circularity and reliability concerns; no human evaluation is conducted, which is standard for controllability/quality claims in visual generation.

Ablations are incomplete: several headline configurations use L=1 particle (Appendices F.2, F.3), which effectively reduces the proposed SMC machinery to plain annealed MCMC, weakening the claim that parallel particle sampling is the key enabler; the benefit of L>1 is only demonstrated qualitatively in Section 4.4.

Compute cost is substantial (4–30 minutes per sample on H200 GPUs, 1–2 GPUs), which limits practicality versus the monolithic baselines and is not analyzed as a compute-matched comparison in all settings.

The conditional sampling approximation (Eq. 7/9) relies on strong assumptions (conditional independence of parent regions, Gaussian deviation of flow predictions) whose validity is asserted rather than empirically characterized; failure modes of expert incompatibility are only discussed in one sentence.

Some claims are stronger than evidence: 'better controllability and output fidelity compared to baselines' is only partially supported (Table 2 shows mixed results, e.g., Traj2V achieves the best LPIPS in the object-centric setting).

strengths: The paper presents a unified and fairly general probabilistic framework (PoE with AIS + SMC) that composes heterogeneous experts—flow/diffusion generative models, autoregressive video models, discriminative VLM rewards, and physics simulators—under one sampling algorithm, which is more general than prior compositional works that focus on homogeneous generators or generator+reward pairs.

The distinction from closely related SMC-based steering work (Skreta et al., 2025; He et al., 2025) is clearly articulated: using per-timestep MCMC kernels that leave p_t invariant rather than accumulating path-wise importance weights, which mitigates weight degeneracy as annealing length grows.

Broad empirical coverage across three application domains (graphics-engine-instructed image editing, physics-simulator-instructed video generation, layout-controlled text-to-image), with appropriate ablations: conditional sampling (Table 1, Fig. 2), SMC resampling (Table 4), and particle count scaling (Table 3) including the L=1 reduction to Du et al. (2023).

Experiments include baselines sharing the same backbone (Add-it, SDEdit, FLUX-Fill, 3DIS-FLUX, Wan2.1-based Image2V/Depth2V/Traj2V), which strengthens fairness of comparisons; compute costs, limitations, and societal impact are transparently reported.
The framework requires only black-box access to discriminative experts (no gradient access), which is a practically valuable property.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The core algorithm (annealed MCMC + SMC resampling for product distributions over diffusion models) is well established (Neal 2001; Doucet et al. 2001; Wu et al. 2023; Singhal et al. 2025; Skreta et al. 2025; Thornton et al. 2025). The claimed technical difference (per-timestep invariant kernels vs. path-wise weights) is a relatively small algorithmic variation, and the paper provides no theoretical analysis quantifying the benefit (e.g., weight degeneracy or bias/variance trade-offs) beyond qualitative argument.

Sampling correctness is only approximate in practice, and the approximations are not rigorously analyzed: the discriminative rewards on noisy samples use Tweedie-style endpoint estimates (r_t(x) ≈ r(x̂)), the conditional-sampling update in Eq. (6) is a heuristic approximation justified only informally in Appendix C.3, regional masking/zero-padding breaks the composed-score interpretation, and K_{t←t+1} does not leave p_t invariant. The paper does not characterize the bias introduced by these deviations.

Evaluation sets are small: 30 scenes for image insertion, 12 scenes for object-centric video, 9 scenes for full-scene simulation, 50 scenes for layout T2I. Given the compute per sample (4–30 min on H200 GPUs), no human evaluation is provided; heavy reliance on GPT-4o automatic scoring (with template prompts) raises concerns about judge bias toward the authors' outputs.

The headline contribution (parallel SMC with discriminative experts) is under-exercised in the main tasks: Section 4.1 uses L=1 (no SMC, no discriminative expert) and Section 4.2 uses L=1 with no conditional sampling due to GPU memory, so the most distinctive components are validated mainly on the smaller Section 4.3 task and appendix ablations.

Some quantitative results are mixed (e.g., SDEdit beats the method on background MSE and ImageReward in Table 1; 'No SMC' sometimes beats SMC on mIoU in Table 4), which the narrative does not fully reconcile; a missing/empty Appendix C.2 on autoregressive instantiation weakens reproducibility for that expert class.

Significance is bounded: the authors acknowledge the method relies on compatible expert predictions, was validated with only a small number of experts, and incurs substantial inference-time cost, limiting the scale at which the framework is currently useful.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem — inference-time composition of heterogeneous models (generative priors, VLM rewards, physics simulators) without retraining — and the framing via product distributions is clean and well-motivated.

The proposed AIS+SMC sampler is a reasonable and sensible algorithmic design; the choice of per-timestep MCMC kernels instead of path-wise importance weights (differing from Skreta et al., 2025 and He et al., 2025) is a defensible practical decision, and the conditional sampling approximation in Eq. (6) is a useful engineering trick for harmonizing region experts.

The evaluation spans multiple tasks (graphics-engine-instructed editing, physics-simulator-instructed video generation, layout-controlled text-to-image generation) with ablations on particle count, conditional sampling, and SMC resampling, and the method shows consistent gains on most controllability and alignment metrics against same-backbone baselines.
The appendix provides reasonable implementation details, compute requirements, limitations, and societal impact discussion.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core ingredients (product-of-experts composition, annealed MCMC, SMC-based reward steering, Feynman-Kac correctors for diffusion) are all well established (Neal, 2001; Du et al., 2020/2023; Wu et al., 2023; Skreta et al., 2025; He et al., 2025). The paper's main claim to novelty — supporting heterogeneous experts and per-timestep kernels — amounts to an incremental combination of known components, and the theoretical contribution is minimal; no analysis of convergence, bias, or when the per-timestep weighting is actually valid.

Evaluation is weak for a top-tier venue: the primary benchmarks consist of only 30 scenes (image editing), 12 scenes plus 9 released PhysGen3D scenes (video), and 50 scenes (layout generation). These tiny, partially self-constructed datasets make many reported differences statistically fragile.

Heavy reliance on automatic metrics of questionable reliability, especially GPT-4o scoring for controllability, quality, and semantic alignment, where improvements are small (e.g., 0.708 vs 0.708 on Table 2) and the protocol is inherited from another paper. No human evaluation or user study is provided, which is essential for claims about 'flexible user interfaces' and 'user controllability'.

Some reported numbers undermine the headline claims: the method's foreground IoU (0.739) is notably lower than the Depth2V baseline (0.787) on the object-centric video task, background MSE is worse than FLUX-Fill, and it only beats 3DIS-FLUX on mIoU by ~0.05 at ~12–25x the compute. The compute cost is substantial (minutes per sample, multiple H200 GPUs), but compute-matched comparisons against strong baselines are largely missing (only a best-of-N variant in the appendix).

The manuscript appears incomplete: Section C.2 (Framework Instantiation with Autoregressive Experts) is essentially empty in the submission despite the autoregressive instantiation being used in Section 4.2 experiments, leaving a key technical component undescribed.

The algorithmic description has correctness gaps: Algorithm 1's resampling step uses approximated log-weights r_t ≈ r(x̂) without formal justification of when the resulting sampler targets p(x), and the conditional sampling approximation (Eq. 6) is heuristic, with the 'justification' in C.3 amounting to another Gaussian assumption rather than an analysis.

Several central claims are stronger than the evidence: 'better controllability than monolithic methods' and 'flexible user interfaces' are asserted but supported only by small-scale quantitative tables and cherry-picked qualitative figures; the impact of key hyperparameters (annealing schedule, w, κ, number of MCMC steps) is not ablated.

The comparisons with closely related work (Skreta et al., 2025; He et al., 2025) are only discussed qualitatively; there is no empirical comparison against these most similar methods, making it impossible to judge whether the proposed weighting scheme actually helps.

strengths: Provides a unified, principled Product-of-Experts framework that composes heterogeneous experts (flow models, autoregressive models, VLM rewards, physics simulators) at inference time without retraining, which is a meaningful step beyond prior works that compose mostly homogeneous generators.

The AIS + SMC sampling algorithm is well-motivated; the distinction from prior SMC-based steering works (per-timestep MCMC kernels leaving p_t invariant vs. path-wise importance weights that risk degeneracy) is clearly articulated.

Experiments span multiple tasks (image object insertion, physics-simulator-driven video generation, layout-controlled text-to-image) with sensible baselines matched to the same backbone (RF-Solver, Add-it, SDEdit, FLUX-Fill, Depth2V/Traj2V/Image2V, 3DIS-FLUX).

Good ablation coverage: conditional sampling (Eq. 6), SMC resampling (Table 4), and particle-count/compute scaling (Table 3) directly support the design choices and show compute-performance tradeoffs.
Broader scope than direct competitors (e.g., combining autoregressive experts and simulator-based constraints in one framework), and limitations and compute costs are honestly reported.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the framework substantially builds on Du et al. (2023), Skreta et al. (2025), and He et al. (2025); the core algorithmic difference (per-timestep kernels vs. path-wise weights) is a relatively thin technical contribution, and much of the system value comes from engineering instantiations on top of strong pretrained backbones (FLUX, Wan2.1, FramePack).

Evaluation sets are very small in places (30 scenes for image insertion, 12 scenes for flow-based video, 9 for full-scene simulation), making the reported gains (often within overlapping std. deviations) statistically fragile.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4o-based automatic evaluation, which is potentially biased and lacks human evaluation; several metrics (ImageReward, VQAScore, aesthetic scores) are imperfect proxies and could favor methods trained/tuned in similar regimes.

Mixed evidence for SMC: Table 4 shows 'No SMC' sometimes achieves better mIoU, and at low compute (L=1) the method's VQAScore (0.567) is far below 3DIS-FLUX (0.800), so the practical advantage only materializes at high compute budgets (4–30 min/sample on H200 GPUs).

Some approximations are heuristic and under-justified: the conditional sampling update (Eq. 6) relies on a Gaussian flow-consistency assumption, and the Gaussian simulator expert with MAP-style gradient updates is a strong simplification.

Appendix quality issues: Section C.2 (autoregressive expert instantiation, referenced from the main text for the Gibbs kernel) appears to be essentially empty, leaving a key component under-documented and hurting reproducibility.
